[Shipping It · Part 5 of 6] ReadMe
Part 5 of Shipping It: the production ML stack. Shipping the model is the start of its problems, not the end of them.
A model’s accuracy almost never falls off a cliff. It erodes, slowly and silently, as the world drifts away from the data it once learned on.
Fraudsters change tactics. A feature pipeline goes stale. A vendor changes a default. None of it throws an error; the service stays green while the predictions quietly rot. This is the post where a statistics background stops being a nice-to-have and becomes the whole job: software engineers watch CPU and memory, but you watch distributions, and you build the alarm that goes off when reality stops looking like training data.

[Part 8 of 9] Building Blocks of Modern AI
This is Part 8 of Building Blocks of Modern AI.
You can’t improve a generative system you can’t measure, and the metrics everyone reaches for first, BLEU and ROUGE, measure word overlap, which is almost unrelated to whether an answer is actually any good. So how do you put a number on quality when there’s no single correct answer to diff against? This post builds the eval discipline that catches what dashboards miss: golden sets you curate by hand, LLM-as-judge calibrated against real human ratings (because an uncalibrated judge is just a confident stranger), and a regression harness that fails CI the day quality silently drops, before your users find it first.

[Part 6 of 9] Building Blocks of Modern AI
This is Part 6 of Building Blocks of Modern AI, and the first application post. It builds directly on attention (Part 4) and optimization (Part 5).
The honest first question almost nobody asks: should you fine-tune at all, or is a good prompt cheaper and better? Often it’s the prompt. This post is about the cases where it genuinely isn’t, and how to fine-tune without renting a cluster. LoRA’s trick is almost suspicious: freeze the entire giant model, then train two tiny matrices whose product is the only thing allowed to move. QLoRA pushes further, quantizing the frozen weights to 4-bit so the whole job fits on a single consumer GPU. We run it end to end on a small open model and let the evals, not a vibe, decide when to stop.

title: 04 · Attention from scratch
text:
[Part 4 of 9] Building Blocks of Modern AI
Part 4 of Building Blocks of Modern AI. We’ve turned text into tokens; now we give the tokens a way to talk to each other.

title: 04 · Attention from scratch
text:
The word that needs context
Here’s a sentence: “The river bank was muddy.” And here’s another: “She deposited the cheque at the bank.”
Same four letters, bank. Two completely different things. You told them apart without noticing, using the words around each one. That’s the whole problem of language in miniature: meaning isn’t in the word, it’s in the company the word keeps.
For years, models were bad at this. RNNs read strictly left to right, squeezing everything seen so far into one fixed memory vector, so by the end of a long sentence the beginning had mostly evaporated.
Attention is the idea that threw that out. It’s so central that the paper introducing the transformer just called it all you need. The move looks obvious in hindsight: instead of compressing the past into a single vector, let every token look directly at every other token and decide, for itself, which ones matter.
So bank, sitting beside river and muddy, leans toward those two, and quietly becomes a different vector than the bank that sits beside cheque.
That’s the entire intuition. The rest of this post is making it precise.

title: 04 · Attention from scratch
section: Q, K, V: a tiny game of question and answer
text:
Q, K, V: a tiny game of question and answer
To let tokens “look at each other,” attention gives every token three jobs, by projecting it three different ways:

Query (\(Q\)): what am I looking for?
Key (\(K\)): what do I have to offer?
Value (\(V\)): and if you pick me, here’s what you actually get.

Picture a room full of people. Each token holds up a query (“I’m the word bank, I’m confused, anyone got context?”), compares it against everyone else’s key (“I’m river, I’m relevant to you”), and the better two match, the more of that neighbour’s value it carries home.
“How well do a query and a key match?” is just their dot product. Compute it for every pair, squash the scores into weights that sum to 1 (softmax), and use those weights to mix the values. Written out, the whole mechanism is one line:
\[\text{Attention}(Q, K, V) = \text{softmax}\!\left(\frac{QK^T}{\sqrt{d_k}}\right)V\]
Don’t let the symbols hide what it is: a weighted average of values, weighted by how much each query matches each key. That’s attention, top to bottom.

title: 04 · Attention from scratch
section: The one detail everyone glosses over: √dₖ
text:
The one detail everyone glosses over: √dₖ
There’s a small divisor in that formula, \(\sqrt{d_k}\), that’s easy to wave off as bookkeeping. It isn’t. Drop it, and training quietly falls apart.
Here’s why. If queries and keys are roughly random with variance 1, their dot product has variance \(d_k\), so in a model with a large head dimension the raw scores swing to big positive and negative numbers. Feed those into softmax and it saturates: one weight goes to ~1, the rest to ~0, and the gradient flatlines. The layer stops learning.
Dividing by \(\sqrt{d_k}\) pulls the scores back to variance 1, keeps softmax in its sensitive range, and the gradients keep flowing. One square root, standing between you and a model that refuses to train.

title: 04 · Attention from scratch
text:
Attention, in fourteen lines
None of this is hand-wavy. It’s short enough to write from scratch:
import numpy as np

def scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, mask=None):
    d_k = q.shape[-1]
    # 1. Scores: how much each query matches each key
    scores = np.matmul(q, k.transpose(-2, -1)) / np.sqrt(d_k)

    # 2. Causal mask: forbid looking at future tokens
    if mask is not None:
        scores += (mask * -1e9)

    # 3. Softmax: turn scores into weights that sum to 1
    weights = np.exp(scores) / np.sum(np.exp(scores), axis=-1, keepdims=True)

    # 4. Mix the values by those weights
    return np.matmul(weights, v), weights
That is the heart of every transformer you’ve ever used. Everything after this is making it faster and cheaper, because the basic version has two expensive habits.

title: 04 · Attention from scratch
section: The bill comes due: the memory wall
text:
The bill comes due: the memory wall
The first habit shows up when a model generates text one token at a time. To produce token \(L+1\), it has to attend to all \(L\) tokens before it, and recomputing the keys and values for that entire history, every single step, is pure waste.
So we cache them. The KV cache stores each token’s \(K\) and \(V\) once and reuses them forever after. Brilliant, except the cache grows with every token and every concurrent request, and it grows fast: for a 70-billion-parameter model with a 128K context, it can swell to tens of gigabytes of fast GPU memory. For most people serving LLMs, this cache, not the math, is what runs out first.
That pressure is exactly why modern models bother with Grouped-Query Attention: instead of every query head carrying its own private key/value, several query heads share one set. Llama 3 does this. You lose almost no quality and you shrink the cache dramatically, a direct answer to the memory wall.

title: 04 · Attention from scratch
section: Why your GPU was sitting idle: Flash Attention
text:
Why your GPU was sitting idle: Flash Attention
The second expensive habit is the \(QK^T\) matrix itself. For a sequence of length \(L\) it’s \(L \times L\), quadratic, and the surprise is where the cost actually lives. It’s not the multiplications. It’s shuttling that giant matrix back and forth between the GPU’s big-but-slow memory and its tiny-but-fast on-chip memory.
Flash Attention fixes it without changing a single number in the result. It tiles the computation: it breaks the huge matrix into blocks small enough to live in fast memory, finishes each block there, and never writes the full thing out. Same math, up to ~3× faster, purely by respecting where the data physically sits. (We’ll meet this memory-versus-compute story again and again.)
We now have a model that can read context. Next: how it actually learns. Loss, gradients, and backpropagation, derived from scratch → Post 05.

title: 02 · Vector search: ANN from scratch
text:

Part 2 of Building Blocks of Modern AI, picking up exactly where Post 01 hit the wall.

title: 02 · Vector search: ANN from scratch
section: A bargain that sounds like cheating
text:
A bargain that sounds like cheating
Post 01 left us staring at a wall. Brute-force search is perfectly accurate and completely doomed: it runs out of our 10 ms budget at around 80,000 documents, and every doubling after that doubles the wait. Wikipedia has six million articles. Real corpora have billions.
So how does anyone search millions of vectors in single-digit milliseconds?
The answer, the first time you hear it, sounds like cheating: stop looking at most of the corpus.
Give up on always finding the exact nearest neighbour. Settle for almost always finding it and, in exchange, skip 99% of the comparisons. That trade has a name, Approximate Nearest Neighbour (ANN) search, and it comes down to a single dial: how much accuracy (recall) will you trade for how much speed (latency)?
The whole craft is giving up as little recall as possible. Three ideas do most of the heavy lifting, and the satisfying part is that they attack from three different angles: where to look, how cheaply to compare, and how to navigate. We’ll build all three.

title: 02 · Vector search: ANN from scratch
text:
Idea 1: Don’t search everywhere (IVF)
Start with the most intuitive move. Hunting for a coffee shop, you don’t scan the planet, you scan your neighbourhood. IVF (inverted file index) does exactly that to the vector space.
Before any query arrives, we carve the space into regions. Run k-means over the corpus to find \(k\) representative centres (centroids); file every document under its nearest centre. Geometrically, this tiles the space into \(k\) patches, a Voronoi partition.
Now a query comes in. Instead of scanning all \(N\) documents, we find the handful of centroids nearest the query and only search inside those tiles.
The single knob is nprobe, the number of tiles you open.
With \(k = 1{,}000\) and nprobe = 1, you look at roughly 0.1% of the corpus. Blistering, but risky: if the query lands near a tile’s edge, its true nearest neighbour might be sitting just across the border, and you’ll never see it. Turn nprobe up and you open more neighbouring tiles; latency climbs roughly linearly, recall climbs fast. That tension is the tradeoff, exposed as a number you can tune.

title: 02 · Vector search: ANN from scratch
text:
Idea 2: Don’t store everything (PQ)
IVF prunes where you search. But a second problem hides underneath: the vectors themselves are fat. Millions of 1,536-dimensional float vectors won’t fit in RAM, and RAM is where speed lives.
Product Quantization is a gorgeous bit of compression. The trick: stop storing vectors, start storing recipes.
Chop each vector into \(m\) short sub-vectors. (A 128-dim vector with \(m = 8\) becomes eight 16-dim chunks.) Now run k-means within each chunk’s slot across the whole corpus, and keep just 256 representative chunks per slot, a little codebook. Every sub-vector is then replaced by the single byte that names its closest codebook entry.
Do the arithmetic and it’s almost rude: a 128-float vector (512 bytes) collapses to an 8-byte code. 64× smaller.
The clever part is search: you never decompress. When a query arrives you precompute its distance to all 256 entries in each slot’s codebook, drop them in a lookup table, and then every document’s distance is just a few table lookups added together. Addition, the thing CPUs do faster than anything else.

title: 02 · Vector search: ANN from scratch
text:
Idea 3: Navigate, don’t scan (HNSW)
IVF and PQ are about pruning and shrinking. The last idea is about movement, and it’s the one most production vector databases actually reach for.
HNSW (hierarchical navigable small worlds) treats the corpus as a graph and turns search into a walk.
The intuition is “six degrees of separation.” In a small-world graph, hardly anyone is your direct neighbour, yet anyone is reachable in a few hops. HNSW stacks that idea into layers, like a skip-list:

Top layers: sparse, with long-range edges, for crossing the whole space in a few big jumps.
Bottom layers: dense, with short edges, for pinning down the exact neighbourhood.

Search drops in at the top, greedily hops toward the query along the long edges, then “falls” a layer and repeats with shorter ones, coarse to fine, until it’s doing a careful local search at the very bottom. You navigate to the answer instead of scanning for it.

That’s why Pinecone, Qdrant, and most vector databases you’ve heard of default to HNSW. The catch, as always, gets paid in memory: all those graph edges have to live somewhere.

title: Prerna Tyagi
section: How I think about the work
text:
How I think about the work
Three lanes, one discipline.
Statistics is the core, not the garnish. Isolation forests, PD curves, embedding distances and attention weights are all the same subject wearing different clothes. When a detection rule needs a threshold, that’s a question about distributions. When an LLM eval disagrees with itself, that’s a question about variance. I trust people who can derive the thing they’re deploying, so I try to be one.
ML that faces real stakes plays by different rules. When a model decides whose account gets frozen, you don’t get to pick a comfortable operating point. A false positive is a real person locked out of their own salary; a false negative is someone’s savings gone. The unglamorous middle is where the real work lives: feature engineering, threshold tuning against costs that aren’t symmetric, and being able to explain exactly why the model flagged the account it flagged.
GenAI and agents are systems, not demos. An agent that produces a beautiful answer once is a demo. An agent that produces an auditable, version-controlled result on a schedule, reliably, is a system, and the gap between the two is where the interesting work lives. Orchestration, retrieval quality, evals, guardrails, lineage. The model itself is maybe 20% of it.

title: 01 · Embeddings & vector search
text:
[Part 1 of 9] Building Blocks of Modern AI
Part 1 of Building Blocks of Modern AI. Each post takes one piece of a modern AI system and rebuilds it from scratch, with code you can run and numbers you can check.

title: 01 · Embeddings & vector search
section: The search box that reads your mind
text:
The search box that reads your mind
Type a few words into a search box that actually understands you, not one that keyword-matches you, and something quietly strange happens underneath.
Your words become a list of numbers. So does every document in the index. Then the machine does geometry: it measures which points sit closest together, and the nearest ones win.
That’s the whole trick behind semantic search, RAG, recommendations, and most of what we now wave at and call “AI.”
The idea is easy. The hard part hides inside two small words: closest, and fast.
So here’s the sentence this entire post is trying to earn:

Given millions of documents and a query, return the nearest neighbours in under 10 ms, on a laptop.

To get there, we have to take two questions seriously that “just use vector search” usually skips right over. What does “close” actually mean, mathematically? And what happens to that 10 ms the moment your corpus stops being a toy?
Let’s start with the first one, because that’s where the magic lives.

title: 01 · Embeddings & vector search
text:
What “close” actually means
Old-school search (BM25, Lucene, the thing inside most databases) matches keywords. Search for sports, and a document that only ever says tennis simply doesn’t come back. The words don’t overlap, so as far as the index is concerned, the two are strangers.
Embeddings refuse to accept that. They map every piece of text to a point in a high-dimensional space where sports and tennis land right next to each other, because the model never really sees the word. It sees the concept.
That’s a nice story. Let me turn it into a number.
Take four sentences, two about gardening and two about finance, and hand them to a small embedding model (all-MiniLM-L6-v2), without ever telling it the topics. Then measure the cosine similarity of every possible pair:
  0.622   'I love plants'              vs  'Gardening is fun'             ← gardening
  0.149   'The stock market crashed'   vs  'Bonds and treasury yields'    ← finance
  0.021   'I love plants'              vs  'The stock market crashed'
  0.016   'I love plants'              vs  'Bonds and treasury yields'
  0.015   'Gardening is fun'           vs  'The stock market crashed'
  0.005   'Gardening is fun'           vs  'Bonds and treasury yields'
Look at the gap. Same-topic pairs sit 30 to 120 times higher than cross-topic ones. Nobody handed the model a label. It drew the border between gardening and finance on its own, purely from having read enough text to know those words live in different neighbourhoods.
But the detail I keep coming back to is subtler than that.
The gardening pair scores 0.62. The finance pair, also “same topic,” scores only 0.15. Why the gap? Because “I love plants” and “Gardening is fun” don’t just share a subject, they share a mood: warm, casual, fond. Whereas “the stock market crashed” (panic) and “bonds and treasury yields” (a dry instrument) share a topic and almost nothing else.
The embedding isn’t matching keywords. It isn’t even really matching topics. It’s matching meaning, and you can read it straight off a single number.

title: 01 · Embeddings & vector search
text:
Three ways to measure closeness
So “close” is the whole game. How do we actually measure it?
An embedding is just a vector \(v \in \mathbb{R}^d\), a point in \(d\)-dimensional space. “Similar meaning” becomes “nearby point,” and there are three ways people usually measure nearby. They’re worth keeping straight, because the choice quietly shows up everywhere downstream.
Dot product is raw alignment: \[\text{Dot}(A, B) = A \cdot B = \sum_{i=1}^{n} A_i B_i = \|A\|\,\|B\|\cos(\theta)\] It folds together both how aligned two vectors are and how long they are. Sometimes that length carries real signal; often it’s noise you’d rather ignore.
Cosine similarity is alignment with the length divided out: \[\text{Cosine}(A, B) = \frac{A \cdot B}{\|A\|\,\|B\|}\] This is the default for text. A long document and a short one about the same thing should point the same direction, even if one vector is “bigger.” Cosine measures direction only.
Euclidean (L2) distance is plain straight-line distance: \[d(A, B) = \sqrt{\sum_{i=1}^{n} (A_i - B_i)^2}\] And here’s a small fact that saves a lot of confusion: once your vectors are normalised to length 1, L2 and cosine produce the same ranking in disguise, because \(\|A-B\|^2 = 2 - 2\cos(\theta)\). Pick whichever your hardware prefers; the order of results won’t budge.
That last identity is also a quiet gift: it means the entire search can be done with one fast matrix multiply. Which raises the obvious question: how fast, exactly?

title: 01 · Embeddings & vector search
section: The simplest thing that works, until it doesn’t
text:
The simplest thing that works, until it doesn’t
There’s a temptation in this field to reach for the clever data structure first. Resist it. The honest baseline is almost embarrassingly plain: embed everything once, and at query time compare the query against every document. No index, no tricks. Exact search.
I ran it on 5,000 real news passages (fancyzhx/ag_news), each a 384-dimensional vector, with the search done as a single normalised matrix multiply.
First, does it even work? Query: “tennis player wins grand slam.” The top result is a passage about Roddick and Federer at the Olympics. The phrase “grand slam” appears nowhere in it. A keyword index would have returned nothing; the embedding walked straight there, because Roddick + Federer + Olympics + gold sits in exactly the right corner of tennis-space.
Then I went looking for where it breaks. You learn more from the misses.
Query: “earnings report from a tech company.” The third result was Limited Brands, a clothing retailer. It has earnings reports, sure, but a tech company it is not. Here’s what happened: the query smuggled in two concepts, and when you average two ideas into one vector, the louder one wins. “Earnings report” simply drowned out “tech company.”
That single wrong answer is the reason production retrieval is never just one matrix multiply. Reranking, query rewriting, hybrid keyword-plus-vector search: every one of those exists to patch the exact failure you just watched happen on result number three.
And the speed? At 5,000 documents, each query took about 0.6 ms. Instant. Which is precisely the trap.

The line is dead straight: about 121 nanoseconds per document, every time. Double the corpus, double the wait, forever.
Put that against our 10 ms budget and it hardens into a ceiling: roughly 83,000 documents, and not one more. English Wikipedia has six million articles. The “instant” search has quietly become a one-second search, and one second is a lifetime.
So brute force isn’t slow. It’s honest: it always finds the true nearest neighbour. It just doesn’t scale. And it’s worth understanding exactly why before we go fixing it.

title: 01 · Embeddings & vector search
section: Why a bigger machine won’t save you
text:
Why a bigger machine won’t save you
The natural instinct is to throw hardware at the wall. It won’t be enough, for two reasons worth keeping.
The first is geometry. As the number of dimensions \(d\) grows, space gets strange. Almost all the volume of a high-dimensional sphere bunches into a thin shell near its surface, which means that for a random spread of points, everything ends up roughly the same distance from everything else. The very notion of “nearest” goes faint. This is the curse of dimensionality, and it’s the deep reason exact search is the only thing guaranteed to be exactly right, and the reason that guarantee costs so much.
The second is more mundane and, in practice, more decisive: memory bandwidth. The bottleneck in vector search usually isn’t the arithmetic. It’s moving the vectors from main memory to the chip that does the math. The distance calculation is cheap; the journey is not. So the algorithms that win are the ones that either move less data, or refuse to look at most of it.
Which is the entire plot of the next post: how to find the nearest neighbours without comparing against everything (IVF, PQ and HNSW, built from scratch) and claw back two orders of magnitude while barely losing any accuracy.
→ Post 02: ANN from scratch

title: 03 · Tokenization: how text becomes numbers
text:
[Part 3 of 9] Building Blocks of Modern AI
This is Part 3 of Building Blocks of Modern AI. Before attention, before embeddings, before any gradient is computed, there is tokenization. It’s the first operation on your input and the last one on your output, and it still gets skipped in most write-ups. That’s a mistake.

title: 03 · Tokenization: how text becomes numbers
text:
The Discrete-Continuous Gap
Neural networks are continuous machines, processing floating-point numbers in high-dimensional spaces. Human language, however, is discrete. Tokenization is the bridge: the lossy, biased, and often brittle process of mapping raw strings into the integers (tokens) that a model can actually “see.”
If the tokenizer is inefficient, the model is blind to patterns, sequences become unnecessarily long, and inference costs skyrocket. And the choices are stranger than they look: by the end of this post you’ll see why the same sentence can cost a model 4–6× more tokens in Hindi than in English, a tax on meaning that nobody designed on purpose. It just fell out of how the vocabulary was built.

title: 03 · Tokenization: how text becomes numbers
text:
The evolution of the unit

The Naive Approach: Word-Level
Split on whitespace: "I love ML" \(\rightarrow\) ["I", "love", "ML"]. - The OOV Problem: What happens to "transformerification"? If it’s not in your 50,000-word vocabulary, it becomes [UNK]. You’ve lost all semantic information. - Vocabulary Explosion: To cover every morphological variation (run, running, ran), you’d need millions of embedding vectors.


The Other Extreme: Character-Level
Split every character: "hello" \(\rightarrow\) ["h", "e", "l", "l", "o"]. - Sequence Bloat: A 500-word paragraph becomes 3,000+ tokens. Given the \(O(L^2)\) cost of attention, this is computationally prohibitive. - The Burden of Spelling: The model must use its capacity to learn that h-e-l-l-o means “hello” before it can learn what “hello” means in context.


The Goldilocks Zone: Subword Tokenization
The industry standard. Common words stay whole ("the", "is"), while rare words decompose into meaningful units ("unhappiness" \(\rightarrow\) ["un", "happi", "ness"]). This ensures a fixed vocabulary size (32K–100K) with zero OOV issues.

title: 03 · Tokenization: how text becomes numbers
text:
Implementing byte-level BPE
Modern LLMs (GPT-4, Llama 3) use Byte-Level Byte-Pair Encoding.

The UTF-8 Detour
Characters in Unicode can be anything from emoji to ancient script. Starting with a vocabulary of every possible character is impossible. Instead, BBPE starts with Bytes (0-255). Every piece of text in every language is just a sequence of bytes in UTF-8.

The Algorithm from Scratch

Initialize: Convert the training corpus into its raw UTF-8 byte sequence.
Count: Find the most frequent adjacent pair of tokens (initially bytes).
Merge: Create a new token for that pair and replace all occurrences.
Iterate: Repeat until your vocabulary size (e.g., 50,257 for GPT-2) is reached.

def get_stats(ids):
    counts = {}
    for pair in zip(ids, ids[1:]):
        counts[pair] = counts.get(pair, 0) + 1
    return counts

def merge(ids, pair, idx):
    new_ids = []
    i = 0
    while i < len(ids):
        if i < len(ids) - 1 and ids[i] == pair[0] and ids[i+1] == pair[1]:
            new_ids.append(idx)
            i += 2
        else:
            new_ids.append(ids[i])
            i += 1
    return new_ids

title: 03 · Tokenization: how text becomes numbers
text:
WordPiece: the statistical competitor
Used in BERT and Gemma, WordPiece differs from BPE in its merge criteria. BPE is greedy about frequency. WordPiece is greedy about Pointwise Mutual Information (PMI).
Instead of merging the most frequent pair, it merges the pair \((a, b)\) that maximizes: \[\text{Score}(a, b) = \frac{P(ab)}{P(a) \cdot P(b)}\]

Intuition: It asks, “Does this pair appear together more often than we would expect by random chance?”
Example: If "t" and "h" are both very common but don’t always appear as "th", their score might be lower than a rarer but highly correlated pair like "q" and "u".

title: 03 · Tokenization: how text becomes numbers
text:
Unigram: the top-down approach
Unlike the bottom-up merges of BPE/WordPiece, Unigram (used in T5 and SentencePiece) starts with a massive vocabulary and iteratively removes tokens.
At each step, it calculates how much the “loss” (likelihood of the corpus) would increase if a token were removed. It keeps the tokens that are most critical to compressing the training data. This allows for probabilistic subword segmentation: the same word can be split in multiple ways during training, which acts as a form of regularization.

title: 03 · Tokenization: how text becomes numbers
text:
The silent inequity: multilingual fragmentation
Tokenization is the root of multilingual performance gaps. Because most tokenizers are trained on English-heavy data:

English: "hello" \(\rightarrow\) 1 token.
Hindi: "नमस्ते" \(\rightarrow\) 18 bytes \(\rightarrow\) ~6 tokens.

The same meaning takes 6x more tokens in Hindi. This means the model has a shorter “effective context window” for Hindi, and Hindi users pay 6x more for the same API call. This is not a model flaw; it’s a tokenizer flaw.

title: 03 · Tokenization: how text becomes numbers
text:
Real-world tooling
In production, you don’t write your own BPE. You use: - tiktoken: OpenAI’s fast Rust-based BPE. - SentencePiece: Google’s implementation that treats whitespace as a character (escaping the need for pre-tokenization). - HuggingFace Tokenizers: The standard for open-source research.
In the next post, we finally implement the heart of the transformer: Post 04: Attention from scratch.

title: 05 · Loss, optimization, backpropagation
text:
[Part 5 of 9] Building Blocks of Modern AI
This is Part 5 of Building Blocks of Modern AI. We’ve built the pieces; now we ask how any of them actually learn.
Every model in this series learns the same way: make a guess, measure how wrong it is, nudge each weight a little in the direction that’s less wrong, and repeat a few million times. That’s the entire loop. “Loss decreases over optimized iterations” isn’t a slogan. It’s the literal algorithm, and backpropagation is just how each individual weight learns its own share of the blame. This post derives backprop end to end on a 2-layer MLP, by hand first, then in code with no autograd hiding the chain rule, and then explains what Adam actually fixes that plain SGD doesn’t, instead of treating the optimizer as a magic word you import.

title: 07 · Retrieval & RAG
text:

This post refuses to pretend retrieval is solved. We build the keyword baseline (BM25, which beats dense retrieval more often than embedding fans like to admit), the dense side from Part 1’s embeddings, the hybrid fusion that combines them, and a cross-encoder reranker on top. title: 09 · Agent loops & tool use
text:
[Part 9 of 9] Building Blocks of Modern AI

A language model generates text. An agent uses that text to do things: call a tool, read the result, decide what to do next, and loop until the job is done. title: 11 · Versioning the unversionable
text:
[Shipping It · Part 2 of 6] ReadMe
Part 2 of Shipping It: the production ML stack. If you can’t reproduce it, you can’t roll it back, and one day you’ll need to.
A bad deploy goes out. You roll back, and Git faithfully restores the code.
Except the thing that just approved a fraudulent transaction wasn’t only code. It was code plus the exact data it trained on, plus the weights that fell out, plus a training run with a random seed and a library version you’ve already upgraded past. Restore the code and you’ve restored one-quarter of the model. This post is about versioning the other three, so that “roll back to last Tuesday’s model” is a command, not an archaeology project.

title: 13 · Serving the model
text:
[Shipping It · Part 4 of 6] ReadMe
Part 4 of Shipping It: the production ML stack. The model is done. Now it has to meet the world, and the world has a latency budget.
In fraud, a model that answers in 200 ms is a useless model. By then the transaction has already cleared; you’re scoring history.
That’s the thing nobody tells you: how you serve a model is a business decision, not a deployment detail. The same model wants three completely different shapes depending on who’s calling it. This post builds all three (the low-latency API behind a live decision, the batch job that scores millions of rows overnight, and the stream that keeps up with a firehose) and shows when each one is the right answer.
